column2: Showering sharp arrows that could stop the lords of elephants, wishing victory in battle, they surrounded the son of Kunti.
Seeing that hero of fierce deeds, all those heroes in chariots fought him, who was on foot.
They struck that hero, the destroyer of the Nivatakavachas, slayer of the Samshaptakas and slayer of the Saindhava.
The seven sages and the divine sages, struck with fear, shed hot tears, filled with grief and sorrow.
A hare, quickly splitting the moon's disc, fell contrary, O king, in that omen.
Clouds like donkey-red, bearing bows and lightning, covering the sky, rained flesh and blood.
So it was then, with the hero covered by showers of arrows, in this world, best of the Bharatas; it seemed a marvel.
Covered on all sides by their net of arrows, Gandiva and the quiver fell from his hand in confusion.
When he had fallen into confusion, the Saindhavas quickly loosed a still greater net of arrows at the great chariot-fighter whose spirit had left him.
Then, knowing Partha bewildered, all the dwellers in heaven were frightened; their minds were pacified for his sake.
Then all the divine sages, the seven sages and the brahmin sages murmured prayers for the victory of the wise Partha.
Then, when Partha's radiance was kindled by the gods, king, the wise one, knower of supreme weapons, stood unmoving in the battle.
Then the delight of the Kurus drew the divine bow, and a great sound came from it again and again, as of a machine.
Then the lord Partha rained showers of arrows from the bow on his enemies, as the lord of the gods rains showers.
Then all those Saindhava warriors and their kings were not seen, covered by arrows, like fires by moths.
They were terrified by his sound, fled afflicted with fear, wept, grieved, and some of the Saindhavas lay down.
The mighty best of men, moving everywhere, engulfed them all in his nets of arrows, O king, like a fire-brand wheel.
That slayer of foes loosed a net of arrows like Indra's net in all directions, like Mahendra bearing the thunderbolt.
Splitting the army like a net of clouds, the best of the Kurus, bright as the sun, shone like the sun in autumn.
Then those Saindhava warriors rallied again, loosing, in great fury, showers of arrows, O Bharata.
Of great valour, Kunti's son, desiring to die as hero, spoke with gentle voice to them as they rallied again:

Fight with all your strength and strive to kill me; do all your tasks; great fear has come to you.
mahabharata:14:77.5	I shall fight you all, warding off your net of arrows; stand with your minds on battle; I shall teach your pride humility.
Having said this, the Kaurava bearing Gandiva, in anger, then, remembering his elder brother's words, O Bharata,
Kshatriyas wishing victory in battle, dear one, are not to be killed but conquered, as the great soul, the king of dharma, said, Phalguna, best of men, then thought.

I was told by the king, 'Kings are not to be killed.' How then could the king of dharma's good word be untrue here?
mahabharata:14:77.9	Let the kings not be killed and the king's command be done. Thinking so, devoted to his brother's welfare, the knower of dharma spoke to the Saindhavas, mad with battle.
Then the Saindhava kings loosed hundreds of thousands of bent-jointed arrows at the wielder of Gandiva.
Dhananjaya cut those cruel arrows, like the poison of venomous snakes, as they blazed, with sharp arrows in mid-air.
Having cut those swift heron-feathered arrows sharpened on stone, he pierced each one of them with ten arrows in the battle.
Then, remembering Jayadratha slain, the Saindhava kings hurled spears and javelins again at Dhananjaya.
The great-minded Kirithin made their purpose vain, cutting all of them in mid-air, and the Pandava shouted with joy.
So too he felled the heads of those warriors rushing in, eager for victory, with bent-jointed broad-headed arrows.
Of those fleeing, then running again, and turning back, the sound was like that of a full ocean.
Struck by Partha of immeasurable radiance, they fought Arjuna with such breath and spirit as they had.
Then, struck by Phalguna with bent-jointed arrows, most of them lost their senses, their horses and soldiers wearied.
Knowing them all worn out, Dhritarashtra's daughter Duhshala took the child, her grandson, the hero, the blameless son of Suratha, and went in a chariot.
For peace for all the warriors she went to the Pandava; reaching Dhananjaya she cried out in distress, and Dhananjaya too, seeing her, put down his bow.
With his bow laid aside, Partha rightly said to his sister, "What shall I do?" and she said to him:
Best of the Bharatas, this is a child, the son of your sister's son; he salutes you, hero; look at him, best of men.
So addressed, Arjuna asked about his father, "Where is he?" Then, O king, Duhshala said:

His father, tormented with grief for his father and overcome with despair, died, hero; hear how it was.
mahabharata:14:77.28	First, having heard his father had been killed by you in battle, blameless one, and hearing that you had come with the horse for battle, tormented by the grief of his father's death, Dhananjaya, he gave up his life.
mahabharata:14:77.29	On hearing only the name 'Bibhatsu has come,' blameless one, my son fell to the earth in despair and died.
mahabharata:14:77.30	Seeing him fallen, lord, I took his son and have come to you today seeking refuge.
Having said this, Dhritarashtra's daughter cried out in distress, and in misery spoke to Partha, who stood with bowed head:

Look on me, your sister, and on my son's son; you should show compassion to me, upholder of the Kurus, forgetting the Kuru king and that fool Jayadratha.
mahabharata:14:77.33	As Parikshit was born from Abhimanyu, slayer of heroes, so this grandson of mine was born from Suratha, mighty-armed one.
mahabharata:14:77.34	Taking him, tiger among men, I have come to you, to pacify all the warriors; hear this word of mine.
mahabharata:14:77.35	This grandson of that fool has come, mighty-armed one; you should show grace to this child.
mahabharata:14:77.36	With me, scourge of foes, he begs you, appeasing you with bowed head, mighty-armed one; be calm, Dhananjaya.
mahabharata:14:77.37	Show grace, knower of dharma, to the child whose kin are slain and who knows nothing; do not come under anger's sway.
mahabharata:14:77.38	Forgetting that ignoble, cruel one and his grandfather, you should show grace to the one who has offended greatly.
As Duhshala so pitifully spoke, Dhananjaya, remembering the goddess Gandhari and King Dhritarashtra, said, grieved and sorrowing, reproaching the kshatriya dharma:
Shame on that mean Duryodhana, greedy for kingdom and proud, for whose sake all my kinsmen were sent to Yama's abode.
Having said this, Jaya made much consolation and grace; embracing her, pleased, he sent her home.
Duhshala, fair-faced, having turned those warriors back from the great battle and honoured Partha, went home.
Then the bull among men, having conquered the Saindhava warriors, again followed that horse that went at will.
The hero followed the sacrificial horse by rule, lord of the people, like the god of gods, bearer of Pinaka, a star-spotted deer in the sky.
And the horse went to those lands as it wished, at ease, increasing Partha's work.
In due course, the horse, going about so, O best of the Bharatas, came with the Pandava to the land of the lord of Manipura.
The wise Dhananjaya did not welcome the lord of Manipura as he arrived, remembering kshatriya dharma.
The righteous Phalguna, angry, said to him: "This reception of yours is not fit, outside kshatriya dharma.
Yudhishthira's sacrificial horse, being guarded, came to your border; why, son, did you not fight me?
Shame on you, ill-minded though skilled in kshatriya dharma, who took me by conciliation when I came for battle.
There is no manliness in you while you live, who took me by conciliation when I came for battle, like a woman.
If I had come to you with weapons laid down, ill-minded one, then your reception would be fit, lowest of men."
Knowing that her husband had said this to him, the serpent's daughter Ulupi, unable to bear it, split the earth and came to him.
She then saw her son, bowed down and thinking, rebuked again and again by her husband who wished for battle, lord.
Putting on golden armour and a shining helmet, he climbed into a great chariot crowded with hundreds of quivers.
It was furnished with all equipment, yoked with horses swift as thought, with fine wheels and gear, decorated with golden vessels, the wise one.
Raising a highly honoured golden lion banner, King Babhruvahana set out toward Partha.
Then the hero, approaching, had the sacrificial horse guarded by Partha seized by men skilled in horse training.
Seeing the horse seized, Dhananjaya, glad, standing on the ground, held back his son in his chariot in battle.
Then that king tormented the hero with thousands of showers of sharp arrows like the poison of venomous snakes.
An incomparable battle took place between father and son, like the battle of gods and asuras, both pleased.
Babhruvahana, tiger among men, laughing, pierced Kirithin at the collarbone with a bent-jointed arrow.
It went with its feathers like a serpent into an anthill, and, piercing the son of Kunti, entered the ground.
Sorely pained, the wise one, leaning on his excellent bow, entered divine radiance, and shone as if intoxicated.
Recovering consciousness and praising his son, Shakra's son, bull among men, said this, lord of the earth:

Well done, well done, mighty-armed child, son of Chitrangada; seeing your deed, so worthy, I am pleased, son.
mahabharata:14:78.26	I release my arrows at you, son; stand firm in battle. Having said this, the slayer of foes rained iron arrows.
The king cut those arrows loosed from Gandiva, bright as thunderbolts, into three each with his iron arrows.
Partha with divine arrows took off by razor-head the golden-adorned banner of his chariot, like a golden palm tree.
And laughing, the best of the Pandavas made the king's huge horses of great speed and valour lifeless.
The king, very angry, quickly got down from the chariot and, on foot, in rage fought his father, the Pandava.
The bull of the Pandavas, pleased at his son's valour, did not much hurt his son, he who was the lowest wielder of thunderbolt.
Babhruvahana, the mighty, though struck, again tormented his father, who was turning away, with arrows like venomous snakes.
Then in childishness Babhruvahana strongly pierced his father in the heart with a sharp, well-feathered arrow.
That arrow, bright with radiance, blazing like fire, entered the Pandava, O king, breaking a vital part and causing great pain.
Struck very sorely by his son, the delight of the Kurus, Dhananjaya, fell to the ground afflicted with faintness, O king.
When that hero, bearer of the burden of the Kauravas, fell, Chitrangada's son too suddenly fell into a faint.
Having fought in the battle, the king, seeing his father slain, and himself having been deeply pierced earlier by Arjuna's showers of arrows,
Chitrangada, seeing her husband slain and her son fallen on the ground, terrified, entered the battlefield.
The fair mother of the lord of Manipura, weeping with a heart scorched by grief, then saw her husband slain.
Recovering consciousness, the goddess of divine form, seeing Ulupi, the serpent's daughter, said this:

Ulupi, look at my husband lying slain in battle, the conqueror in war, by my young son for your sake.
mahabharata:14:79.4	Are you not, noble lady, a knower of dharma, and a devoted wife, that for your sake he has fallen, your husband slain in battle?
mahabharata:14:79.5	If all the fault is this Dhananjaya's today, forgive, I beg you; revive Dhananjaya.
mahabharata:14:79.6	Are you not, noble lady, a knower of dharma, known in the three worlds, fair one, that having had your husband killed by a son you do not grieve?
[Ulupi] "I do not grieve for my son slain, daughter of the serpent; I grieve only for the husband for whom this hospitality was done."
Having said this to the goddess Ulupi, the serpent's daughter, the renowned one, approaching her husband, said this:
Rise, you who please the foremost of the Kurus; this horse, mighty-armed one, has been released by me for you.
[Chitrangada] "Ulupi, look well at my husband slain in battle; having urged this son and had him killed, you do not grieve.
Let this child sleep on the ground, gone the way of the dead; let the red-eyed Gudakesha Vijaya live well.
It is no fault for men to have many wives, fortunate one, but it is for women; let not such a thought be yours.
This friendship was made by the Creator, eternal and imperishable; understand it as friendship; let your agreement be true.
If you do not show me my husband alive today, having had him killed by his son, I shall give up my life.
Afflicted by sorrow, timid one, bereft of husband and son, I shall fast to death right here as you watch, without doubt."
Having said this to her co-wife, the serpent's daughter, Chitrangada then sat fasting, silent, O lord of the people.
Then, recovering consciousness, King Babhruvahana, looking at his mother on the battlefield, said:

What is more sorrowful than this, that my mother, raised in comfort, lies by the dead hero, her husband, fallen on the ground?
mahabharata:14:80.4	The slayer of enemies in battle, best of all weapon-bearers, was killed by me in the fight, and she watches; alas, death is hard.
mahabharata:14:80.5	Ah, this goddess's heart must be firm, that it does not split as she looks on her husband slain, with broad chest and mighty arms.
mahabharata:14:80.6	I think death is hard for man here, since on the road not yet reached neither I nor my mother are parted from life.
mahabharata:14:80.7	Alas, shame! See the golden armour on the Kuru hero's chest thrown on the ground, of one slain here by me, his son.
mahabharata:14:80.8	O brahmins, look at my father, the hero, lying on the hero's bed on earth, felled by me, his son.
mahabharata:14:80.9	Let the brahmins appointed for the foremost of the Kurus, followers of the horse, perform the pacifying rite today for him who was greatly struck in battle.
mahabharata:14:80.13	Look, best of serpents' daughters, at my husband slain by me; I have done what pleases you today, having slain Arjuna in battle.
mahabharata:14:80.14	I too shall go today by the road frequented by the ancestors; I cannot bear to hold up myself by myself, fair one.
mahabharata:14:80.15	So you, mother, when I am dead and the bearer of Gandiva is dead, be pleased, goddess; I swear by truth.
Having said this, the king, struck by grief and sorrow, touched water, great king, and in pain said:

Let all beings, moving and unmoving, hear, and you too, mother; I speak truly, best of serpents.
mahabharata:14:80.18	If my father, the Bharata bull, does not rise, I shall dry up my body right in this battlefield.
mahabharata:14:80.19	For there is no atonement anywhere for me after killing my father; I shall surely go to hell, tormented by the killing of my teacher.
mahabharata:14:80.20	By killing a kshatriya hero one is freed by a hundred cows, but having thus killed my father the atonement is hard for me.
mahabharata:14:80.21	This one, the greatly radiant son of Pandu, Dhananjaya, and my righteous father: the atonement for him has been made by me.
Having said this, O king, the son of Dhananjaya, the great-minded, touched water and sat silent, ready to fast to death.
Then Ulupi thought of the reviving jewel, and that refuge of serpents appeared.
Taking it, Kaurava, the daughter of the lord of nagas then said to the soldiers words that gladdened the mind.

Rise, son; do not grieve; this Jishnu was not killed by you; he cannot be conquered by men or by gods with Vasava.
mahabharata:14:81.5	This illusion, called Mohini, was employed by me for the pleasure of your father, the renowned lord of men.
mahabharata:14:81.6	For this Kaurava, slayer of heroes, wished to test your strength, son; he did not come fighting in the war, king.
mahabharata:14:81.7	Therefore you were urged by me to fight, son; do not suspect sin in yourself even slightly, lord.
mahabharata:14:81.8	This is a sage of great radiance, an eternal, imperishable Person; not even Shakra could defeat him in battle, son.
mahabharata:14:81.9	This divine jewel has been brought by me, lord of the people, which always revives dead serpent kings.
So addressed, he placed the jewel on Partha's chest, he of immeasurable radiance, out of love for his father, putting off the sin.
When the jewel was placed, hero, Jishnu, the lord, was revived and rose as if awakened from sleep, his eyes red and wiped.
Seeing that great-souled, high-minded one risen and conscious, his father healthy, Babhruvahana saluted him.
When the tiger among men rose again glorious, Pakashasana, lord, rained holy divine flowers.
Unstruck kettledrums sounded with the voice of clouds, and a great sound of "Well done, well done" arose in the sky.
The mighty-armed Dhananjaya, risen and comforted, embraced Babhruvahana and kissed his head.
Then Dhananjaya saw not far off his mother, thin with grief, standing with Ulupi, and asked:

What is this, all seen at once with grief, wonder and joy on the battlefield, scourge of foes? If you know, tell me.
mahabharata:14:81.19	Why has your mother come to the battlefield, and why has this Ulupi, the serpent king's daughter, come here?
mahabharata:14:81.20	I know that this battle was done by you at my word; I wish to know the reason for the women's coming.
Asked, the lord of Manipura then replied, appeasing him with bowed head: "Ask Ulupi."
[Arjuna] "Are you well-wishing, daughter of the serpent, toward this king or me, fickle-eyed one? Do you wish us well?
Broad-hipped one of fair looks, have I done you any displeasure through ignorance, or has this Babhruvahana?
And has the princess Chitrangada, your co-wife, the fair-hipped Chaitravahini, done you any wrong?"
The daughter of the lord of serpents, smiling, said to him: "You have not offended me, nor has King Babhruvahana, nor this mother of his, who stands like my servant.
Hear what I have done and how; you should not be angry with me; I appease you with my head.
For your pleasure, Kaurava, this was done by me, blameless one; hear it all, mighty-armed Dhananjaya.
In the war of the Mahabharata, because you killed King Shantanu's son unrighteously, Partha, this is the atonement made for it.
For Bhishma was not felled by you in fair fight, hero; he was fighting while Shikhandin was joined to him, and you killed him relying on him.
This was heard before, as the Vasus told me, when, Shantanu's son the king having been killed, they came to the bank of Ganga.
The Vasus, bathing in the great river and gathering, said this terrible word, with the approval of Bhagirathi.
'This Shantanu's son Bhishma was slain by Savyasachin while not fighting in battle, attached to another, fair one.
For that offence we too, fair one, shall join Arjuna with a curse,' and she said, 'So be it.'
I told my father that, greatly distressed, and he, hearing it, fell into great despair.
My father went to the Vasus for your sake and begged again and again; having appeased them, they said this:
'Again the young lord of Manipura, his son, will fell him with arrows to the ground in the middle of battle.
When this is done, king of serpents, he will be freed from the curse. Go,' said the Vasus; and he told me this.
Hearing that, I freed you from that curse; not even the king of the gods could defeat you in battles.
One's son is held to be oneself; therefore you were defeated by him here; I think there is no fault in me; or how do you think, lord?"
So addressed, Vijaya, glad in soul, said this: "All that you have done is very pleasing to me, goddess."
Having said this, Jaya said to his son, the lord of Manipura, as Chitrangada and the king's daughter listened, Kaurava:
Yudhishthira's horse sacrifice will be on the full moon of Chaitra; come there with your ministers and with your two mothers, king.
Thus addressed by Partha, King Babhruvahana, with eyes full of tears, the wise one, said to his father:

Knower of dharma, I shall come by your command to the great horse sacrifice, as a server of the twice-born.
mahabharata:14:82.27	But for my favour, enter your own city with both wives, slayer of foes; let there be no doubt in this.
mahabharata:14:82.28	Having lived here free of arrows, happy in your own house, lord, you can follow the horse again, best of conquerors.
Thus addressed by his son, the ape-bannered son of Kunti, smiling, said then to Chitrangada's son:

You know, mighty-armed one, how I am keeping my vow; I shall not enter your city yet, broad-eyed one.
mahabharata:14:82.31	The sacrificial horse goes as it wishes; good fortune to you; I shall go; I have no abiding place.
There, duly honoured by him, Indra's son, permitted by his two wives, the best of the Bharatas, set out.
The radiant wearer of the diadem, following the horse, turned back and by chance came to the royal city.
As he came near, the king, grandson of Jarasandha, standing in kshatriya dharma, called him to battle.
Then Meghasandhi came out of the city in a chariot, with bow, arrows and gloves, and attacked Dhananjaya, who was on foot.
Reaching Dhananjaya, the greatly radiant Meghasandhi, out of childishness, O great king, not from skill, said this:

Why is this horse being led, Bharata, as if among women? I shall take this horse; strive to release it.
mahabharata:14:83.7	If you have not been given consent in war by my fathers, I shall give you hospitality, or I strike.
Thus addressed, the Pandava replied, smiling: "I have laid down the vow that one who creates obstruction must be stopped by me.
It is surely known to you too, king, from my elder brother; strike as you can; there is no anger in me."
So addressed, the lord of Magadha struck the Pandava first, scattering thousands of arrows like the thousand-eyed pours rain.
Then the brave bearer of Gandiva effortlessly made those arrows vain with arrows sent from Gandiva, best of the Bharatas.
Having made his flood of arrows vain, the ape-bannered one loosed blazing arrows like fiery-mouthed serpents.
They fell on the banner, flagpoles, chariot-machine and horses, and on other parts of the chariot, but not on his body or his charioteer.
Protected by Partha in his body, the Magadhan, thinking it his own valour, sent arrows at Phalguna.
Then the brave bearer of Gandiva, struck by the Magadhan, shone like a great spring palasha in flower.
Not killed, the Magadhan struck the best of the Pandavas; and he stood so, O Kaurava, in the sight of the world's hero.
But Savyasachin, enraged, drawing his bow strongly, made the horses lifeless and cut off the charioteer's head.
With a razor-head he cut his great varied bow, and felled the quiver-case, flag and banner.
The king, troubled, horseless, bowless and charioteerless, took a mace and rushed swiftly at Kunti's son.
As his gold-adorned mace came on, he cut it into many pieces with many vulture-feathered arrows.
That mace, split into pieces, its jewelled bindings scattered, fell from him in a thousand parts, like a snake being let go.
Arjuna, the wise leader in battle, did not wish to strike him, chariotless, bowless and mace-less.
Then the ape-bannered one said gently to him, who stood dejected in kshatriya dharma:

This kshatriya dharma has been enough shown, son; go. This is much work in battle for you, a boy, king.
mahabharata:14:83.25	Yudhishthira's instruction is that kings are not to be killed; therefore you live, king, though you offended me in battle.
Its gates should be made large, ample, well divided on every side and guarded by engines.
Without the Vrishni hero and the Madhus, uncle, I cannot bear to see the earth for long here, lord.
Having dismissed those brahmins, King Janamejaya then returned from Takshashila to Gajahvaya.
